title: Creating arrays
blurb: np.array turns lists and tuples into ndarrays; nested brackets add dimensions, ndmin forces extra ones, and ragged rows are rejected.

notes.0: numpy is imported once under the usual alias np.
notes.1: A tuple works just like a list: a 1-D array with 5 elements, shape (5,).
notes.2: Two inner lists of equal length become a 2-D array: 2 rows x 4 columns, shape (2, 4).
notes.3: ndmin=3 wraps the data in extra brackets until the array has 3 dimensions: shape (1, 1, 5).
notes.4: Three levels of brackets = 3-D array, shape (2, 2, 2): 2 blocks, each 2 rows x 2 columns.
notes.5: The rows have different lengths (4 and 5), so NumPy cannot build a rectangular array and raises ValueError.

title: Array attributes
blurb: ndim, shape, size, dtype, itemsize and nbytes describe an array without changing it.

notes.4: size = total number of elements = 2 x 4.
notes.5: dtype = type of every element. Integers default to int64 on 64-bit macOS/Linux (the PDF shows int32, which is the Windows / older-NumPy default).
notes.6: itemsize = bytes used by ONE element (int64 -> 8).
notes.7: nbytes = size x itemsize = 8 x 8 = 64 bytes.
notes.8: Any float in the data makes the whole array float64.

title: Built-in array builders
blurb: zeros, ones, eye, diag, arange and linspace build arrays without typing every value.

notes.1: np.zeros(5): five 0.0 values. The default dtype is float64.
notes.2: np.ones((3, 4)): pass the shape as a tuple - 3 rows x 4 columns of 1.0.
notes.3: np.eye(3): identity matrix - 1 on the diagonal, 0 elsewhere. Only one size argument is needed.
notes.4: np.diag([2, 3, 4, 5]): puts the list on the diagonal of a 4x4 matrix; ints stay ints.
notes.5: np.arange(start, stop, step) works like range(): stop (10) is excluded.
notes.6: np.linspace(1, 6, 5): 5 evenly spaced numbers from 1 to 6 - stop IS included.
notes.7: num=5 spaces five values from 0 to 10: step = (10-0)/(5-1) = 2.5.

title: Choosing a dtype
blurb: The second argument of np.array sets the type code: b, B, i, I, f, F, ? and the text types S, U, O.

notes.1: 'b' = signed byte -> int8 (1 byte per element).
notes.5: 'f' = float -> float32 (note the dtype shown in the repr).
notes.7: '?' = boolean: every non-zero number becomes True.
notes.8: 'S' = byte string (|S1): each number becomes b'1', b'2' ...
notes.10: 'O' = Python object: elements stay ordinary Python ints.
notes.11: 129 does not fit in int8 (-128..127). The PDF shows it wrapping to -127; NumPy 2.x refuses with OverflowError instead.

title: Indexing and slicing
blurb: Integer indexes pick elements, slices cut ranges; a slice keeps dimensions, an integer drops one.

notes.5: Chained indexing gives the same value but builds temporary arrays; ar3_1[1, 1, 1] is the better style.
notes.7: An integer index on the first axis drops that dimension: 1-D row [5 6 7 8].
notes.8: A slice 1:2 keeps the dimension: still 2-D, shape (1, 4).
notes.9: 0:2:1 selects both rows: the whole 2-D array.

title: reshape and flatten
blurb: reshape gives a new shape (without assignment the change is temporary); flatten always returns a 1-D copy.

notes.2: The array is 1-D with 12 elements: shape (12,).
notes.3: reshape(4, 3) returns a 4x3 array but nothing stores it - this change is temporary.
notes.5: Assign the result to keep it - this change is permanent. 3 x 2 x 2 = 12 elements.
notes.6: flatten() turns any array into a new 1-D array.
notes.7: 5 x 3 = 15 is not 12 - the total number of elements must stay the same.

title: resize and transpose
blurb: resize changes the array itself (in place); transpose swaps axes and does nothing on a 1-D array.

notes.2: resize(11) works IN PLACE: arr is cut to 11 elements (the 12 is dropped).
notes.3: transpose() of a 1-D array does nothing - there is no second axis to swap.
notes.4: resize(12) grows it back; the new slot is filled with 0.
notes.6: transpose() swaps rows and columns: (3, 4) becomes (4, 3).

title: View or copy?
blurb: reshape returns a view that shares memory with the original; flatten returns an independent copy.

notes.2: b is a 2x3 VIEW: it reads the same memory as a (see the shares-memory marker).
notes.3: Writing through the view changes a as well - same memory.
notes.4: flatten() copies the data: c is independent.
notes.5: Changing c leaves a and b alone.
